name: Slow-Motion Video Input Lag Meter
title: Slow-Motion Video Input Lag Meter (120fps / 240fps) | Toolkit Gen
description: Measure end-to-end display latency and controller input lag using smartphone slow-motion video recordings with frame-by-frame timestamp analysis.
author: ToolkitGen Engineering Team
quickAnswer: The Slow-Motion Video Input Lag Meter turns any modern smartphone camera into an optical latency testing tool. By stepping frame-by-frame through a 120fps or 240fps slow-motion recording of your physical finger actuating a button and the screen reacting, it calculates exact end-to-end system input latency in milliseconds with jitter confidence bounds. All video decoding occurs locally in browser memory without server uploads.
features: Local In-Memory Video Processing (Zero Cloud Uploads for Complete Privacy)
Two-Point Visual Timestamp Marking: Mechanical Actuation to First Pixel Shift
Sub-Millisecond System Latency Calculation with Rolling Shutter Jitter Intervals
Standardized Optical Diagnostic Report Export for Gaming Communities

howTo.name: Record Your Test Video
howTo.text: Record a slow-motion video (120fps or 240fps) on your smartphone showing both your controller/mouse button and the screen in the same frame.

howTo.name: Load Video Locally
howTo.text: Drag and drop the video file into the browser workspace. The file processes entirely within local RAM.

howTo.name: Select Recording Frame Rate
howTo.text: Confirm your smartphone's slow-motion framerate (typically 120fps or 240fps on modern iOS and Android devices).

howTo.name: Mark the Button Contact Frame
howTo.text: Use the frame stepper buttons to pause on the exact frame where your finger initiates physical contact.

howTo.name: Mark the Pixel Reaction Frame
howTo.text: Step forward until the first pixel change (gunfire, jump, cursor movement) appears on the display panel.

faq.q: How accurate is testing input lag with a smartphone slow-motion camera?
faq.a: Extremely accurate when calibrated properly. At 240 frames per second, each individual frame represents exactly 4.17 milliseconds of real-world elapsed time (1,000 ms / 240 fps). The resulting measurement error is bounded by ±2.08 ms, which rivals multi-thousand-dollar hardware oscilloscope setups [Confirmed: Optical latency testing methodologies].

faq.q: Does my video file get uploaded to ToolkitGen servers?
faq.a: No. All video decoding, playback, and canvas frame grabbing execute locally in your browser memory using HTML5 Video and browser memory object URLs. Tool inputs are processed locally on your device.

faq.q: What is the difference between button-to-pixel lag and button-to-USB lag?
faq.a: Button-to-USB latency only measures peripheral switch scan time (typically 1ms to 8ms). Button-to-pixel (total system latency) measures the full pipeline: peripheral debounce + USB transmission + game engine render tick + GPU queue + video cable transmission + display panel scanout.

faq.q: How does smartphone rolling shutter affect latency measurement?
faq.a: CMOS smartphone cameras read sensor rows sequentially from top to bottom (rolling shutter). To minimize optical rolling shutter distortion, position your finger and the reacting portion of the screen along the same horizontal scanline in the camera frame.

articleHtml:
Optical Input Lag Methodology: Slow-Motion Frame Analysis

Measuring total system latency—from physical button actuation to the first displayed pixel reaction—historically demanded specialized LED photodiodes and high-speed hardware oscilloscopes. High-framerate slow-motion video enables high-precision optical latency verification with zero external hardware.

The Mathematics of Optical Timing

When recording at a constant high frame rate ($FPS$), each individual frame represents an exact, fixed temporal window (the frame interval, $\Delta t$):

$$\Delta t = \frac{1,000\text{ ms}}{\text{Camera Frame Rate (FPS)}}$$

By counting the total discrete frames ($\Delta F$) elapsed between the physical contact of the controller switch and the earliest luminance shift on the display panel, end-to-end latency ($L$) is calculated directly:

$$L = \left( \frac{\Delta F}{\text{Camera Frame Rate}} \right) \times 1,000\text{ ms} \quad \pm \left(\frac{\Delta t}{2}\right)$$

At 240 FPS (standard on iPhone 13 through iPhone 16 and Samsung Galaxy S21 through S24 devices [Confirmed: Hardware specifications]), each frame equals $4.167\text{ ms}$. If 6 frames elapse, total latency is $25.0\text{ ms} \pm 2.08\text{ ms}$.

Rolling Shutter Calibration Guidelines

Smartphone CMOS cameras read scanlines sequentially from the top of the sensor to the bottom (rolling shutter). If the controller is at the top of the camera frame and the screen reaction is at the bottom, sensor scanout delay can introduce an artificial measurement skew of $2\text{ms}$ to $4\text{ms}$.

  • Horizontal Alignment: Align your finger/controller and the reacting area of the display on the same horizontal plane in the camera frame.
  • Sufficient Lighting: High-speed recording requires fast shutter speeds (e.g., 1/1000s). Ensure the testing area is brightly lit with continuous DC LED lighting to prevent 50Hz/60Hz AC light bulb flickering.
Measurement Notice: Optical measurement results reflect total end-to-end hardware latency including switch travel time, peripheral debounce, USB bus scheduling, GPU render pipeline, and panel pixel transition. ToolkitGen is an independent platform.
